title: Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guahan
backgroundAndFacts:
The United States military undertook a massive buildup on the island of Guam, relocating thousands of Marines from Okinawa, Japan, and constructing new training ranges and facilities. This buildup required federal environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), a law that requires federal agencies to study and disclose the environmental effects of major projects before they proceed. Prutehi Guahan (formerly known as Prutehi Litekyan), an environmental advocacy group based in Guam, sued the Department of the Air Force and other federal agencies, arguing that the environmental review was inadequate—that it failed to properly analyze the significant impacts the buildup would have on Guam's land, water, coral reefs, and Indigenous Chamorro communities.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guahan, finding that the environmental review was deficient and ordering the agencies to take a harder look at the project's impacts. The federal government appealed to the Supreme Court, raising questions about the scope of NEPA's requirements as applied to U.S. territories, which are governed by a complex patchwork of constitutional doctrines known as the Insular Cases. Guam is an unincorporated U.S. territory, meaning its residents are American nationals but not all constitutional rights automatically apply there in the same way they do in the fifty states.

The case has attracted significant attention from a wide range of interests. Business groups and several Republican-led states argue that the Ninth Circuit's ruling imposes excessive procedural burdens on federal agencies, threatening military readiness and large infrastructure projects. Environmental groups, Democratic-led states, community organizations from U.S. territories, and some Members of Congress have sided with Prutehi Guahan, arguing that people in territories deserve the same environmental protections as those on the mainland.
legalQuestion: Whether the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) requires federal agencies to analyze environmental impacts on U.S. territories—specifically Guam—using the same standards applied to the continental United States, and whether a Guamanian environmental group has standing to challenge a military buildup's environmental review.
significance:
This case has major implications for how environmental law applies in U.S. territories, home to roughly four million American nationals in places like Guam, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands. A ruling in favor of the federal government could mean that residents of these territories receive weaker environmental protections than people living in the fifty states, even when the federal government itself is the one undertaking the project causing environmental harm. It also implicates the longstanding but controversial Insular Cases doctrine, which has historically allowed the government to treat territories and their residents differently from states.

Beyond the territorial context, the case could reshape how NEPA applies to large federal projects more broadly. Business groups and the government argue that expansive NEPA requirements slow down military construction, energy projects, and infrastructure development nationwide. A ruling that narrows what agencies must analyze in their environmental reviews could have sweeping consequences for environmental law across the country, while a ruling affirming the Ninth Circuit could reinforce robust environmental review obligations for major federal undertakings.

parties.party: Department of the Air Force, et al.
parties.coreArgument: The federal government argues that the Ninth Circuit imposed overly demanding environmental review requirements that go beyond what NEPA actually requires, threatening military readiness and disrupting a carefully planned strategic buildup in the Pacific. The government contends that its environmental review was thorough and legally sufficient, and that courts should defer to agencies' reasonable judgments about the scope and depth of environmental analysis. They also argue that extending expansive NEPA obligations to U.S. territories without regard to their distinct constitutional status is legally unwarranted.
supportingPoints: The environmental review conducted by the military was comprehensive and met all requirements under NEPA and applicable regulations.
Courts owe deference to agency judgments about how to scope and conduct environmental reviews of complex military projects.
Imposing heightened NEPA obligations on military construction in territories undermines national security and Pacific deterrence strategy.
The Ninth Circuit's standard would require agencies to conduct virtually endless analysis, making large federal projects practically infeasible.

parties.coreArgument: Prutehi Guahan argues that the military's environmental review failed to take the required 'hard look' at the severe and lasting impacts the Guam buildup would have on the island's environment and Indigenous communities, as NEPA plainly requires. The organization contends that residents of Guam are entitled to the same meaningful environmental review protections as Americans on the mainland, and that allowing the government to cut corners on environmental analysis in territories would leave some of the most vulnerable American communities without legal recourse. They maintain that the Ninth Circuit correctly applied longstanding NEPA principles in finding the review inadequate.
supportingPoints: NEPA requires agencies to rigorously analyze all significant environmental impacts, including cumulative effects on Guam's fragile coral reef ecosystems and freshwater resources.
The military's review improperly minimized or ignored the disproportionate burdens the buildup would impose on Indigenous Chamorro communities.

Residents of U.S. territories are entitled to meaningful NEPA protections because the federal government owes the same environmental review obligations regardless of where in U.S. jurisdiction a project occurs.
The Ninth Circuit applied standard, well-established arbitrary-and-capricious review and found clear deficiencies in the agency's analysis that courts are obligated to correct.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This is one of the foundational 'Insular Cases' establishing that the Constitution does not automatically apply in full to U.S. territories, which is central to the dispute over whether NEPA's requirements apply equally to Guam.

This case defines the scope of an agency's obligation to prepare a programmatic environmental impact statement covering an entire region, which is relevant to arguments about how broadly the military had to analyze the Guam buildup's regional effects.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case established the 'arbitrary and capricious' standard of judicial review for agency decisions under the Administrative Procedure Act, the standard the Ninth Circuit applied when finding the military's environmental review deficient.

citedPrecedents.caseName: Robertson v. Methow Valley Citizens Council
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: This case clarifies NEPA's procedural requirements, including what an adequate environmental impact statement must contain, and is frequently cited by both sides to define the 'hard look' standard agencies must meet.

This foundational standing case defines what a plaintiff must show to sue in federal court, which is relevant to whether Prutehi Guahan can demonstrate the concrete injury, causation, and redressability required to challenge the environmental review.

The Court's most recent engagement with the Insular Cases confirmed that Congress may treat territories differently from states in certain respects, which the government cites to argue that different environmental review standards in territories are constitutionally permissible.
